title: Every loop kind: ten challenges
idea: Pick the loop that matches the job: `do...while` for at least one pass, `for...in` for object keys, nested loops for combinations.

analogy.text: A car odometer. The right-most digit runs through 0 to 9 completely before the next digit moves up by one.
analogy.breaks: Digits always cycle 0 to 9; an inner loop's length can vary.

points: `do...while` runs its body, then tests: it always makes at least one pass.
`for...in` visits each key of an object; read its value with `obj[key]`.
In nested loops, the inner loop finishes all its passes for each outer pass.
A plain `for` fits index work, such as steps of 2 or walking backwards.

steps.caption: Next inner pass: `n` is 2. The outer loop waits on `'A'`.
`n` is 3: the last inner pass for `'A'`.
`n` becomes 4, so `n <= 3` is false. The inner loop ends.
The outer loop moves on: `row` is `'B'`. `n` no longer exists; the inner loop will start over.
A new inner loop begins with `n` at 1 again and adds `'B1 '`.
The passes for `n` 2 and 3 add `'B2 '` and `'B3 '`.
Both loops are done. The body ran 2 x 3 = 6 times, and `console.log` prints all six seats.

code.title: do...while and for...in
code.caption: Run it. Change `tries < 0` to `tries < 3` and predict what the `do...while` prints.

challenges.intro: Each prompt names the loop to use. Run the tests, and open a hint only when you are stuck.

items.title: Count the digits
items.prompt: Write `countDigits(n)` using `do...while`. `n` is a whole number, 0 or more. Return how many digits it has; `0` has one digit.
hints: A plain `while` would skip the body for `0`. `do...while` always runs once, which suits the one digit of `0`.
Each pass drops the last digit: `Math.floor(n / 10)` divides by 10 and rounds down. Add 1 to a counter per pass.
`do { n = Math.floor(n / 10); count++; } while (n > 0);` then `return count`.

items.title: Keys that are true
items.prompt: Write `enabledFlags(flags)` using `for...in`. Return an array of the keys whose value is exactly `true`, in the object's order.
hints: `for (const key in flags)` gives one key per pass. The value is `flags[key]`.
A value like `1` is truthy but not `true`. Compare with `=== true`.
Make an empty array before the loop, `push(key)` when the test passes, and `return` the array after the loop.

items.title: Total a cart
items.prompt: Write `cartTotal(items)` using `for...of`. Each item is `{ price, qty }`. Return the sum of `price * qty` over all items; an empty cart gives `0`.
hints: `for (const item of items)` gives one object per pass. Read its fields as `item.price` and `item.qty`.
Start `total` at `0` and add one item's `price * qty` on every pass.
`for (const item of items) { total += item.price * item.qty; }`, then `return total` after the loop.

items.title: Triangle of stars
items.prompt: Write `triangle(n)` using nested loops. Return an array of `n` strings: `'*'`, then `'**'`, then `'***'`, and so on. For `n` below 1, return `[]`.
hints: The outer loop makes one row per pass. The inner loop builds that row.
Row number `i`, counting from 1, has `i` stars, so the inner loop runs `i` times.
Per outer pass: start `let row = ''`, add `'*'` in the inner loop, then `rows.push(row)`. Return `rows` last.

items.title: Every pair in order
items.prompt: Write `pairs(items)` using nested loops. Return an array of `[a, b]` arrays: each item paired with every item after it. For `[1, 2, 3]` that is `[[1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]]`.
hints: The outer loop picks `a` by index `i`. The inner loop picks every `b` that comes after it.
Start the inner loop at `i + 1`, not at 0, so no item pairs with itself and no pair repeats.
`for (let j = i + 1; j < items.length; j++)` inside the outer loop, with `result.push([items[i], items[j]])`.

items.title: Stop at a negative
items.prompt: Write `sumBeforeNegative(numbers)`. Add the numbers in order and use `break` to stop at the first negative number. `0` is not negative.
hints: A loop normally runs to the end. `break` leaves it at once.
Test each number first: if it is below 0, `break`. Otherwise add it to the total.
`for (const n of numbers) { if (n < 0) break; total += n; }`, then `return total`.

items.title: Skip the non-numbers
items.prompt: Write `sumNumbers(values)`. Use `continue` to skip every item whose `typeof` is not `'number'`. Return the sum of the numbers that remain.
hints: `continue` ends the current pass early and starts the next one.
At the top of the body: if `typeof v !== 'number'`, `continue`. The code below it only sees numbers.
`for (const v of values) { if (typeof v !== 'number') continue; total += v; }`, then `return total`.

items.title: Reach 1 with while
items.prompt: Write `collatzSteps(n)` using `while`. While `n` is not 1: halve it if it is even, otherwise set it to `3 * n + 1`. Return the number of steps. `n` is 1 or more.
hints: You cannot know the number of passes in advance, so `while (n !== 1)` fits better than a counting `for`.
Inside the loop, test `n % 2 === 0`. Change `n` in the `if` branch or the `else` branch, then add 1 to `steps`.
Inside `while (n !== 1)`: halve or triple-plus-one `n` with `if`/`else`, then `steps++`. Return `steps` after the loop.

items.title: Every other item
items.prompt: Write `everyOther(items)` using a `for` loop that steps by 2. Return a new array with the items at index 0, 2, 4, and so on.
hints: The last part of a `for` can be any change. `i += 2` moves two places each pass.
Start at `i = 0` and keep going while `i < items.length`.
`for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i += 2) { picked.push(items[i]); }`, then `return picked`.

items.title: Is it a palindrome?
items.prompt: Write `isPalindrome(text)` using a `for` loop with two counters that move toward each other. Return `true` if `text` reads the same backwards. Case matters; `''` is a palindrome.
hints: Compare the first and last characters, then the second and second to last, moving inward.
`for (let i = 0, j = text.length - 1; i < j; i++, j--)` runs two counters at once.
Inside, `return false` when `text[i] !== text[j]`. After the loop, `return true`.

pitfalls: Give nested loops different counters, `i` and `j`; a repeated name hides the outer one.
In a `while` loop, change the counter before `continue`, or the loop never ends.
To stop two nested loops at once, `return` from the function; `break` leaves only one.

quiz.why: The body runs once before the first test. `n` becomes 6, then `6 < 3` is false and the loop ends.

takeaway: Before you loop, ask: at least once? Keys or values? One loop or two?

starters: When would I really need a do...while loop?
What is the difference between for...in and for...of?
How do I break out of two nested loops at once?
